Setting (from the previous page): x is defined implicitly by x = t + u·X with X = f(x), which is Lagrange's equation. φ = φ(x) is arbitrary. Subscripts below denote partial derivatives in t and u. Equations already established there:
(1) φ_u = X φ_t, obtained from x_u = X x_t.
(2) X_u = X X_t, which is (1) with φ = X.
(3) φ_tu = X_t φ_t + X φ_tt, from differentiating (1) in t.
(4) φ_uu = ∂_t(X² φ_t).
The previous page ended with φ_uuu = ∂_t∂_u(X² φ_t).

This page:
(a) The order of mixed partial differentiation is immaterial, so φ_uuu = ∂_t[∂_u(X² φ_t)].
(b) Product rule: ∂_u(X² φ_t) = 2X X_u φ_t + X² φ_tu.
(c) Substitute (2) and (3) (my explicit expansion): 2X·X X_t φ_t + X²(X_t φ_t + X φ_tt) = 3X² X_t φ_t + X³ φ_tt = ∂_t(X³ φ_t).
(d) Hence (5): φ_uuu = ∂_t²(X³ φ_t). 'Likewise' φ_uuuu = ∂_t³(X⁴ φ_t), and so on.
(e) General lemma (6): ∂_u(Xⁿ φ_t) = ∂_t(X^{n+1} φ_t). The check (implicit, mine): n X^{n-1} X_u φ_t + Xⁿ φ_tu = n Xⁿ X_t φ_t + Xⁿ(X_t φ_t + X φ_tt) = (n+1) Xⁿ X_t φ_t + X^{n+1} φ_tt = ∂_t(X^{n+1} φ_t).
(f) Induction (7): suppose ∂ⁿφ/∂uⁿ = ∂_t^{n-1}(Xⁿ φ_t). Differentiate in u and commute ∂_u past ∂_t^{n-1}. Then apply (6) to get ∂^{n+1}φ/∂u^{n+1} = ∂_t^{n-1} ∂_u(Xⁿ φ_t) = ∂_tⁿ(X^{n+1} φ_t). So the law holds for the next term.
(g) Conclusion: (1), (4), (5) give the formula for the first three terms, and (6) gives it for all subsequent ones.

Purpose: this is the key lemma for the Lagrange inversion series. Note that Xⁿ φ_t = f(x)ⁿ φ'(x) x_t = ∂_t ∫ f(x)ⁿ φ'(x) dx. At u = 0 we have x = t, so ∂ⁿφ/∂uⁿ|_{u=0} = dⁿ⁻¹/dtⁿ⁻¹ [f(t)ⁿ φ'(t)]. The Taylor series in u then gives φ(x) = φ(t) + Σ uⁿ/n! dⁿ⁻¹/dtⁿ⁻¹ [f(t)ⁿ φ'(t)]. The next page (headed 'Lagranges Lehrsatz') carries out exactly this step.
errors: In the line after substituting (2) and (3), the term written as X³ d²φx/(dt du) should be X³ d²φx/dt². The final equality with d(X³ dφx/dt)/dt holds only with φ_tt. This is a notational slip; the result is correct.
The text says (6) follows 'durch die Substitution (3) u. (4)'. The substitutions actually needed are (2) and (3), as in the n = 2 case earlier on the page. This is a reference slip.
The notation (dφx^n/du^n) stands for dⁿφx/duⁿ. It is idiosyncratic, not an error.
The interchange of the order of partial differentiation is taken as 'bekanntlich' (well known). Analytic or smooth dependence is tacitly assumed, which is acceptable for the period.
The step 'Man findet ebenso' for n = 4 is asserted, not computed. It is subsumed by the general induction.

results.what: For x = t + u f(x): ∂φ/∂u = f(x) ∂φ/∂t and ∂(f(x)ⁿ ∂φ/∂t)/∂u = ∂(f(x)^{n+1} ∂φ/∂t)/∂t. Hence ∂ⁿφ/∂uⁿ = ∂ⁿ⁻¹/∂tⁿ⁻¹ (f(x)ⁿ ∂φ/∂t), proved by induction.
results.modern_name: Laplace's partial-differential proof of the Lagrange inversion theorem (Lagrange–Bürmann series)
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1770) for the series; Laplace (1777/1780) for this PDE-based proof via ∂z/∂u = f ∂z/∂t
